title: SYSK Selects: How Currency Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode "How Currency Works." Chuck introduces it as his pick, noting it covers all kinds of currency, not just money. The hosts open with personal banter about childhood collections (coin dispensers, banks, comics), then discuss the New York Magazine story on liquid Tide being used as currency in drug trades. The episode traces the history of currency: barter problems, commodity money (cacao beans, cattle, cowrie shells), the invention of coins in Lydia and China, Roman debasement, early paper money in China, Sweden and the gold-backed goldsmith notes, the gold standard and The Wizard of Oz allegory, electronic money and the first credit card, perception of value and devaluation, the Big Mac Index, supply and inflation, Weimar Germany hyperinflation and the Rentenmark, etymology of money words (buck, fee, dollar, salary, shell out, simoleon), and a listener mail shout-out to Bree Bagnal for her first wedding anniversary.
topics: The Wizard of Oz gold standard allegory

segments.title: Opening banter and childhood collections
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the episode as his Selects pick. The hosts reminisce about childhood collections of coin dispensers, piggy banks, comics, baseball cards and Sports Illustrated.

segments.title: Liquid Tide as black market currency
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a New York Magazine article describing liquid Tide being stolen and used as a currency to buy drugs in the United States. They define currency as an agreed-upon medium of exchange and compare it to cigarettes, honey buns and deerskins.

segments.title: Barter problems and why currency emerged
segments.summary: Currency solved barter problems such as finding a trading partner and making change. Money could also store wealth, since perishable goods like corn rot while gold does not. This shifted power toward a merchant class.

segments.title: Commodity currency: cacao beans, cattle and goats
segments.summary: The hosts describe four categories of currency and focus on commodity currency. Examples include cacao beans used by the Aztecs, which Spanish conquistadors discarded, and the practical downsides of bulky or perishable goods like cattle and goats.

segments.title: Origins of coins in Lydia and China
segments.summary: Coins first appeared in Lydia, in modern Turkey, under King Croesus around the seventh century BC. In China, coinage developed from tool-shaped currency with holes that were kept in later round coins. The hosts note the fiat nature of money and that gold has limited practical use.

segments.title: Roman debasement, paper money and gold-backed notes
segments.summary: Governments gained control of the money supply, and Roman emperors debased coinage, contributing to their decline. Paper money started in China, failed in Sweden in 1661 through oversupply, then caught on in the eighteenth century from goldsmith receipts that became gold-backed paper currency.

segments.title: Gold standard and The Wizard of Oz
segments.summary: US dollars were backed by gold until the gold standard was abandoned, with the hosts placing the shift in the 1930s and officially in 1971. They mention the Wizard of Oz as a populist allegory for the gold standard and Milton Friedman's view that currency has value because people believe it does.

segments.title: Electronic money and credit cards
segments.summary: Electronic money grew out of bank records transfers after World War Two. Diners Club introduced the first credit card in 1950, and the Social Security Administration began electronic deposits. The hosts discuss trust in electronic payments and the decline of checks.

segments.title: Devaluation, Big Mac Index and supply and demand
segments.summary: Currencies fluctuate through deliberate devaluation and perception of value. The Economist's Big Mac Index compares purchasing power across countries. Supply and demand drive inflation and deflation.

segments.title: Weimar Germany hyperinflation and the Rentenmark
segments.summary: After World War One, Germany printed money to pay reparations and reached extreme hyperinflation in 1923. The hosts describe the resulting zero stroke condition, and say the currency was stabilized with the Rentenmark backed by land and industrial assets. They link the instability to the rise of fascism.

segments.title: Cowrie shells and etymology of money words
segments.summary: Cowrie shells were used as currency for about two thousand years, mainly from the Maldives, and their value rose the farther they traveled toward China. The hosts then discuss the etymology of buck, fee, dollar, salary and shell out, and the origin of the word simoleon.

segments.title: Listener mail: shout-out to Bree Bagnal
segments.summary: Listener Jared Bagnal asks for a shout-out to his wife Bree, a devoted listener, for their first wedding anniversary. The hosts read the mail and wish the couple well.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to get in touch through social media and email, and to visit the website.
